alsoSee.why: A private survey of factory purchasing managers. A reading above 50 usually means manufacturing is expanding; below 50 means it is contracting. You will see this in the Full calendar; it is not a U.S. government release, so we do not date it here.
alsoSee.how: Compare the headline index with 50, and with what was expected. A surprise move across 50 gets more attention than a small change while already above or below.
alsoSee.hint: A stronger PMI is typically a mild plus for stocks, especially industrials; a weaker one can be a mild minus. Typical, not guaranteed.

alsoSee.why: The same idea as the manufacturing PMI, but for the much larger services side of the economy. Also a private survey, listed in the Full calendar.
alsoSee.how: Above 50 generally means services are expanding; below 50, contracting.
alsoSee.hint: A stronger reading is typically friendlier for stocks; a weaker one less so. Typical, not guaranteed.

alsoSee.why: Another private purchasing-managers’ survey, often published a little before the ISM figures. Readings above 50 point to expansion. “Flash” is an early estimate; “final” is the revised one.
alsoSee.how: Read it the same way as ISM: 50 is the dividing line between expansion and contraction.
alsoSee.hint: Surprises can nudge stocks and the dollar, usually less than CPI or jobs. Typical, not guaranteed.

alsoSee.why: A private estimate of private-payroll changes, usually the day before the official jobs report. It can set the tone, but it often disagrees with the official number.
alsoSee.how: The headline is jobs added or lost, in thousands. Treat it as a hint, not a substitute for the official jobs report.
alsoSee.hint: A surprise can move stocks modestly ahead of the official report. Typical, not guaranteed.

alsoSee.why: A private survey of how optimistic households feel about the economy and jobs. Sentiment can hint at future spending, but it is not spending itself.
alsoSee.how: The headline is an index. Higher means more confidence; lower means less. Compare with the previous reading and with what was expected.
alsoSee.hint: A big drop can be a mild headwind for retailers and the broader market; a jump can be a mild plus. Typical, not guaranteed.

alsoSee.why: Another private household survey, with a preliminary reading mid-month and a final one later. It also asks about inflation expectations, which the Fed watches.
alsoSee.how: Higher sentiment is more optimistic; lower is more cautious. Inflation-expectation figures can matter as much as the headline mood.
alsoSee.hint: A sharp drop, or a jump in inflation expectations, can nudge bonds and stocks. Typical, not guaranteed.

jobs.official: Employment Situation (nonfarm payrolls and unemployment rate)
jobs.plain: Monthly jobs report: how many jobs the economy added, and the unemployment rate
jobs.why: This is the most-watched snapshot of the U.S. job market. It can move stocks, bond yields and the dollar within seconds, and it often shapes what traders expect the Federal Reserve will do with interest rates.
jobs.how: The headline jobs number is how many payrolls were added (or lost) last month, in thousands. The unemployment rate is the share of people looking for work who do not have a job. A much stronger report than expected (more jobs, or a lower unemployment rate) is often read as a hotter economy. A much weaker report is read as a cooling one. The two numbers can disagree.
jobs.hint: A hotter jobs report can lift stocks when it signals a healthy economy, but it can also keep interest rates higher for longer, which can weigh on stocks. A weaker report can do the opposite. Options often get pricier (higher implied volatility) into this morning and cheaper after the number is out — that drop is called IV crush. These are typical patterns, not guarantees.

cpi.plain: Consumer prices (CPI): how fast prices for everyday goods and services rose last month
cpi.why: CPI is the best-known inflation report. Inflation affects what things cost, what the Fed may do with interest rates, and how expensive options can become around the release.
cpi.how: The usual headlines are the monthly percent change in the CPI and in “core” CPI (which leaves out food and energy). Higher than expected means prices rose faster than economists looked for; lower means inflation was cooler.
cpi.hint: Hotter-than-expected inflation is typically a headwind for both stocks and bonds, because it can keep rates higher for longer. Cooler inflation is typically friendlier. This is one of the biggest days for option prices: implied volatility often jumps before the release and drops afterward, even if the first stock-market move is sharp. Typical, not guaranteed.

ppi.plain: Producer prices (PPI): what companies are paying for goods and services, before those costs reach shoppers
ppi.why: PPI is an earlier look at inflation in the production pipeline. It usually moves markets less than CPI, but a surprise can still shift rate expectations.
ppi.how: Read the monthly percent change, and the core figure that leaves out food and energy. Higher than expected means costs in the pipeline rose faster; lower means they cooled.
ppi.hint: A hotter PPI is typically a mild headwind for stocks and bonds; a cooler one is typically friendlier. It rarely moves option prices as much as CPI or the jobs report, unless the surprise is large. Typical, not guaranteed.

pce.official: Personal Income and Outlays (includes the PCE price index)
pce.plain: Personal spending and inflation (PCE): how much households earned and spent, and the inflation gauge the Fed watches most
pce.why: This Bureau of Economic Analysis report includes the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index — the inflation measure the Federal Reserve says it pays the most attention to — plus income and spending.
pce.how: Traders focus on the monthly change in the PCE and core PCE price indexes, and on whether spending is holding up. Higher inflation than expected is “hotter”; lower is “cooler.” Strong spending with cool inflation is often read as a Goldilocks mix.
pce.hint: A hotter PCE reading is typically less friendly for stocks and bonds; a cooler one is typically more friendly. The idea is the same as CPI, usually with a slightly softer market reaction. Implied volatility can still rise into the release. Typical, not guaranteed.

gdp.plain: GDP: a revised look at how fast the U.S. economy grew last quarter
gdp.why: GDP is the broadest scoreboard for the economy. The first “advance” estimate is revised twice; later prints can still move markets if they change the story. Corporate profits are often published with the second or third estimate.
gdp.how: The headline is usually the annualized percent change in real GDP for the quarter. Faster than expected means the economy grew more quickly; slower means it cooled. Look at whether the revision is up or down from the previous estimate.
gdp.hint: A stronger GDP print can support stocks when it signals healthy growth, but very strong growth can also keep the Fed cautious on rate cuts. A much weaker print can weigh on stocks in the moment and raise hopes of easier policy. Typical, not guaranteed.

claims.plain: Weekly jobless claims: how many people filed for unemployment last week
claims.why: This is a fresh, weekly pulse on the job market. It is less of a market-mover than the monthly jobs report, but a sudden jump can rattle stocks and boost expectations of Fed rate cuts.
claims.how: The headline is new (“initial”) claims, usually in thousands of people. A higher number means more people filed for unemployment — a softer job market. A lower number suggests a still-solid one. The four-week average smooths a noisy week.
claims.hint: A sharp rise in claims can be soft for stocks in the moment but friendlier for rate-cut hopes. A drop can do the opposite. This weekly print rarely moves option prices as much as CPI or jobs day, unless the change is unusually large. Typical, not guaranteed.
claims.sourceName: U.S. Department of Labor, Employment and Training Administration

jolts.official: Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS)
jolts.plain: Job openings (JOLTS): how many positions employers were trying to fill
jolts.why: JOLTS shows how tight the labor market is. A lot of unfilled openings can mean employers are still competing for workers, which can keep wage growth — and inflation pressure — in the conversation.
jolts.how: The headline is the number of job openings, usually in millions. Higher than expected means more openings (a tighter market); lower means the hiring demand cooled. The quits rate is a secondary clue about how confident workers feel.
jolts.hint: More openings than expected can be read as a still-hot job market, which is mixed for stocks if it keeps the Fed cautious. Fewer openings can ease those worries and sometimes help bonds. Typical, not guaranteed.

retail.official: Advance Monthly Sales for Retail and Food Services
retail.plain: Retail sales: how much people spent in stores and restaurants last month
retail.why: Consumer spending is a large part of the U.S. economy. A surprise here can change the growth outlook and, with it, expectations for company earnings and interest rates.
retail.how: The headline is the monthly percent change in retail sales. “Control group” or “ex-autos” figures strip out noisy categories. Higher than expected means shoppers spent more; lower means they pulled back.
retail.hint: Stronger spending is typically friendly for stocks, especially retailers, unless it is so strong it fans inflation worries. Weaker spending is typically a headwind. Typical, not guaranteed.

housing.plain: Housing starts: how many new homes builders began last month
housing.why: Housing is sensitive to interest rates. Starts and building permits tell you whether builders are pushing ahead or pulling back.
housing.how: The headline is housing starts, usually as a seasonally adjusted annual rate (how many homes that monthly pace would add up to over a year). Higher than expected means more building; lower means less. Permits are a look at plans in the pipeline.
housing.hint: More starts than expected are typically friendly for homebuilders and, in a gentle way, for stocks; fewer starts can weigh on those groups. The broad market reaction is usually modest. Typical, not guaranteed.

durable.official: Advance Report on Durable Goods Manufacturers' Shipments, Inventories, and Orders
durable.plain: Durable goods orders: demand for long-lasting manufactured goods, such as machinery and aircraft
durable.why: This is an early read on business investment. Aircraft and defense orders can swing the headline around, so many people also watch the figure that excludes transportation, or “core capital goods.”
durable.how: The headline is the monthly percent change in new orders. Higher than expected means more demand; lower means a pullback. A single large aircraft order can distort the headline, so check the ex-transportation number when you can.
durable.hint: A stronger report is typically a mild plus for industrial stocks; a weaker one is a mild minus. It is less of an options-volatility event than CPI or jobs day. Typical, not guaranteed.

newsales.plain: New home sales: how many newly built homes were sold last month
newsales.why: New-home sales show whether buyers are still stepping up at today’s mortgage rates. It complements housing starts, which measure building, not buying.
newsales.how: The headline is new homes sold, as a seasonally adjusted annual rate. Higher than expected means more sales; lower means fewer. The median sale price is a secondary clue.
newsales.hint: Stronger sales are typically friendlier for homebuilders and related stocks; weaker sales can weigh on them. The broad market usually takes this in stride. Typical, not guaranteed.

construction.plain: Construction spending: how much was spent on building projects last month
construction.why: This adds up residential, commercial and public construction. It is a useful backdrop for the economy, but it rarely moves markets on its own.
construction.how: The headline is the monthly percent change in total construction spending. Higher means more building activity; lower means less.
construction.hint: A surprise here is typically a small move for construction-related stocks and a muted one for the broader market. Typical, not guaranteed.

eci.plain: Employment Cost Index: how fast what employers pay in wages and benefits is rising
eci.why: The Fed watches labor costs as a clue to inflation that may last. A hot ECI can keep rate-cut hopes in check; a cool one can ease them.
eci.how: The headline is the quarterly percent change in total compensation, and often the wages-and-salaries piece. Higher than expected means labor costs rose faster; lower means they cooled.
eci.hint: A hotter ECI is typically a mild headwind for stocks and bonds; a cooler one is typically friendlier. Typical, not guaranteed.

trade.official: U.S. International Trade in Goods and Services
trade.plain: International trade balance: the gap between what the U.S. exported and imported
trade.why: A wider deficit (more imports than exports) can trim GDP; a narrower one can add to it. The report also offers a look at global demand for U.S. goods.
trade.how: The headline is the trade balance in billions of dollars. A more negative number is a wider deficit; a less negative (or a surplus) is narrower. Look at whether exports or imports drove the change.
trade.hint: A narrower deficit is typically a small plus for the growth picture; a wider one a small minus. The day is usually quieter for option prices than CPI or jobs. Typical, not guaranteed.
trade.sourceName: U.S. Census Bureau and U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis

productivity.plain: Productivity: how much output workers produced per hour, and what that labor cost
productivity.why: Rising productivity can let the economy grow without as much inflation pressure. Unit labor costs are the cost side of the same coin.
productivity.how: Headlines are the quarterly percent change in productivity and in unit labor costs. Higher productivity is usually welcome; faster labor-cost growth can raise inflation worries.
productivity.hint: Stronger productivity is typically a mild plus for the inflation outlook and for stocks; faster unit labor costs can be a mild minus. Typical, not guaranteed.

fomc.official: Federal Open Market Committee interest-rate decision
fomc.plain: Fed interest-rate decision: whether the Federal Reserve is raising, cutting, or holding its policy rate
fomc.why: The Fed’s policy rate influences borrowing costs across the economy — mortgages, business loans, and the discount rate used in almost every stock and option model. The statement, and the chair’s press conference, can matter as much as the rate itself. Meetings marked with projections also include the “dot plot.”
fomc.how: The decision is usually announced at 2:00 p.m. ET (1:00 p.m. CT). Markets also read the wording of the statement and, at projection meetings, the Summary of Economic Projections. A “hawkish” surprise means the Fed sounds firmer on inflation or rates; a “dovish” surprise means it sounds more open to easier policy.
fomc.hint: A more hawkish decision or statement is typically a headwind for stocks and a plus for the dollar; a more dovish one is typically friendlier for stocks. Option prices often stay elevated into the announcement and can drop afterward (IV crush), especially if the decision matches what was expected. Typical, not guaranteed.
fomc.sourceName: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

fomc-minutes.official: Minutes of the Federal Open Market Committee
fomc-minutes.plain: Fed meeting minutes: a detailed write-up of what officials discussed at the last rate meeting
fomc-minutes.why: The minutes come out three weeks after a meeting and can reveal disagreements or a shift in tone that was not obvious on decision day.
fomc-minutes.how: There is no single number. Readers look for whether officials sounded more worried about inflation or about growth, and for any discussion of future rate moves. Released at 2:00 p.m. ET (1:00 p.m. CT).
fomc-minutes.hint: A more hawkish-than-expected tone can weigh on stocks; a more dovish one can support them. Moves are usually smaller than on decision day. Typical, not guaranteed.
fomc-minutes.sourceName: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
